title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together
description: Brute force to optimized: recounting zeros from scratch for every candidate window versus a fixed-size sliding window that adjusts the zero count incrementally.

content.title: Minimum Swaps to Group All 1's Together

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a binary array data, return the minimum number of swaps required to group all 1s present in the array together, in any one contiguous block, using swaps between any two elements.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The final block of 1s has a FIXED size, the total count of 1s in the array","A fixed-size sliding window, sized exactly to the number of 1s"],["A swap is needed for every 0 sitting inside the eventual block","Minimizing the zero count inside a sliding window of that fixed size"]]}

blocks.text: Count the total number of 1s in data, call it k. The 1s will eventually occupy some contiguous block of k positions. Any 0 currently sitting inside that block needs one swap (with a 1 currently outside it) to be moved out. Find the block of size k with the fewest 0s, since that block needs the fewest swaps.

blocks.title: Analogy: Consolidating Scattered Coins Into One Pile of a Known Size
blocks.text: Picture coins scattered among empty spaces in a row, and knowing in advance exactly how large the final coin pile must be (the total number of coins). Sliding a window of exactly that size across the row and counting the empty spaces inside it reveals how many coins from outside would need to be swapped in to fill it.

blocks.caption: A window sized to the total count of 1s; every zero inside it costs one swap

blocks.text: There are 3 ones total. The windows of size 3 are [1,0,1] (1 zero), [0,1,0] (2 zeros), and [1,0,1] (1 zero); the minimum is 1 swap.
There is only 1 one total. A window of size 1 can be placed directly on that single 1, containing 0 zeros, so 0 swaps are needed.
Edge case: data contains no 1s, or is entirely 1s
When there are no 1s to group, or every element is already a 1, 0 swaps are needed.
Before trying to simulate swaps directly, notice that grouping the 1s together is equivalent to choosing where a fixed-size block should sit.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: However the 1s end up grouped, that final block occupies exactly k contiguous positions, where k is the total count of 1s, since no 1s are created or destroyed.

Observation 2: For any candidate block of size k, every 0 currently inside it must be swapped out for a 1 currently outside it, one swap per zero, and this is exactly achievable (a 1 outside always exists to trade with a 0 inside, since the total 1 count matches the block size).

Observation 3: So the number of swaps needed for a given block position exactly equals the number of zeros currently sitting inside it.

Observation 4: Trying every possible block position and taking the one with the fewest zeros gives the true minimum swap count.
This reduces the problem to: slide a window of size k (the total count of 1s) across the array, and find the position with the fewest zeros inside it.
Count the total ones k, then for every possible window of size k, count the zeros inside it directly, and track the minimum.

items: Count k, the total number of 1s in data.
For every starting index i from 0 to data.length minus k, count the zeros in data[i .. i+k-1] directly.
Track the minimum zero count seen across every window.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recount zeros from scratch for every window

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: k is computed once, up front, since it fixes the required window size for every candidate block.
Every candidate window is scanned independently, with no memory carried from the previous window.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), recounting k elements for each of roughly n windows.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: neighboring windows overlap in all but one element, so recounting every window from scratch repeats almost all of the previous window's work.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recounting is wasteful: sliding the window by one position only changes one element on each end, the rest of the window is identical.

What update is actually needed: add 1 to the zero count if the newly entering element is a 0, subtract 1 if the element just leaving the window was a 0.

The core idea: count zeros in the first window once, then slide and adjust in O(1) per step, tracking the minimum seen.

Count the zeros in the first window of size k directly. Then slide the window forward one position at a time, adding 1 to the zero count if the entering element is a 0, and subtracting 1 if the leaving element was a 0, tracking the minimum zero count seen.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: adjust the zero count by exactly the entering and leaving elements

blocks.text: Since sliding the window by one position always changes exactly one element on each end, adjusting the zero count by just those two elements always produces the exact zero count for the new window, matching a full recount without ever repeating the shared work.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass across the array.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: The key insight is realizing the final grouped block has a fixed, known size (the total count of 1s), which turns "minimum swaps" into "minimum zeros in a fixed-size window," a direct fixed-size sliding window problem.

items: Trying to simulate actual swaps instead of recognizing the problem reduces to counting zeros in a window.
Forgetting the early exit when there are no 1s, or the array is entirely 1s, both need 0 swaps.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["All zeros","0 swaps, there are no 1s to group."],["All ones","0 swaps, already one contiguous block."]]}

blocks.text: Explaining why the swap count for a candidate block equals exactly its zero count, since a 1 outside the block is always available to trade for each zero inside it, is the key justification to state clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how do swaps relate to a window", think: the final block has a fixed size, the total count of 1s, and each zero inside a candidate block costs one swap.

items: How would this change if the array were circular, allowing the block to wrap around the end?
Why is one swap always sufficient to move a 1 into a zero's position inside the window?
Fixed-size sliding window problems in general, where a running count is maintained incrementally rather than recomputed.
The circular variant of this same problem, which extends the window to wrap around the array.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n times k) time; the optimized sliding window runs in O(n) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: fixed-size sliding window, sized to the total count of 1s, minimizing the zeros inside it.
Core Idea: the minimum swap count for a candidate block equals its zero count, so slide a window of that fixed size and find the minimum.
Time: O(n times k) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized sliding window.
Most Important Observation: the eventual block of grouped 1s always has a fixed, known size, the total count of 1s.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the swap-to-window reduction is recognized.
One line memory trick: slide a window sized to the ones count, minimize the zeros inside it.
